prayer.text: Saint John Francis Regis, pray for us.

cues.text: A Merchant's Son Chooses Poverty

Jean-Francois Regis was born on January 31, 1597, at Fontcouverte in southern France, the son of a wealthy merchant recently ennobled for his service during the wars of religion that had torn France apart in the previous century.
Rather than pursue the comfortable career his father's newly acquired status could have secured him, Regis entered the Jesuit novitiate at Toulouse in 1616.
Classmates later recalled that an ascetic seriousness marked him even during his years of study.
He avoided the ordinary diversions of student life and gave himself instead to prayer and disciplined study of rhetoric and philosophy.
A Missionary to His Own Country

Ordained in 1630, Regis spent the following decade as a missionary not to some distant land but to rural France itself, where decades of religious war between Catholics and Protestant Huguenots had left whole regions poorly catechized and pastorally neglected.
He crossed some fifty districts on foot, often subsisting on little more than apples and bread while preaching in village squares.
He heard confessions for hours at a stretch and ministered especially to prisoners, children, and the rural poor whom more comfortable clergy rarely reached.
Lace and Dignity

Regis became particularly known for his work among women trapped in prostitution, a ministry he approached not with denunciation but with practical concern for how a woman could actually leave that life and support herself afterward.
He established safe houses and taught many of the women he helped the trade of lacemaking.
This gave them a skilled, respectable livelihood rather than good intentions and no means of independence.
That combination of spiritual and practical charity earned him, centuries later, recognition as the patron saint of lacemakers.
Death in a Winter Confessional

By the winter of 1640 Regis was already suffering from a serious lung ailment, but he refused to curtail a planned parish mission at La Louvesc, insisting on preaching and hearing confessions despite his declining strength.

A penitent eventually found him unconscious in the confessional itself; revived long enough to receive the last rites, he died within hours, on December 31, 1640, at only forty-three years old, having spent barely a decade in active ministry.
Legacy
Pope Clement XII canonized Regis in 1737, nearly a century after his death.
Marking the fourth centenary of his birth in 1997, Pope St. John Paul II praised the 'lofty figure of holiness' who had led an 'immense crowd' back to Christ in so brief a ministry.
Regis is remembered today as a secondary patron of the Diocese of Kansas City–St. Joseph, Missouri, and his name marks schools, parishes, and a university across the world.
We recognize in him a model for anyone tempted to think real missionary work requires distant, exotic fields.
Regis found his mission field in his own countrymen, forgotten by a Church too often occupied elsewhere.
He gave everything he had, down to his last conscious hour, to reach them.
